When stones become lodged in one of the ureters, this condition is known as ureterolithiasis. Diagnosis is made with a noncontrast CT scan of the abdomen. Acute management depends on the size of the stone and the presence of complicating factors such as concurrent ascending urinary tract infection or altered anatomy.

questionStem: A 25-year-o ld man is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after collapsing near the completion of a 26-mile run in warm, humid weather. On arrival, he is obtunded and warm. His temperature is 40.5 °C (104.9°F), pulse is 120/min and regular, respirations are 40/min, and blood pressure is 85/50 mm Hg. Examination shows moist, clammy skin. Laboratory studies show: Hematocrit 55% Leukocyte count 15,000/mm 3 (15 x 109/L) with a shift to the left Platelet count 55,000/mm 3 (55 x 109/L) Serum Urea nitrogen Creatinine Alkaline phosphatase AST ALT Creatine kinase 50 mg/dL (17.8 mmol/L) 2.5 mg/dL (221 µmol/L) 100 U/L 500 U/L 500 U/L 1000 U/L Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Heat stroke is characterized by an increased body temperature that occurs when the body is exposed to high environmental temperatures and high humidity, and it commonly occurs in young athletes or in elderly patients with impaired thermoregulatory capacity. Excessive heat exposure and increased core body temperature leads to cardiovascular and neurologic dysfunction with secondary tachycardia, tachypnea, and hypotension. Vasodilation of superficia l blood vessels may lead to multi-organ system failure, including hepatic and renal ischemia, rhabdomyo lysis, and disseminated intravascular coagulation. Treatment includes cooling of the patient with fans or ice water, continuous core temperature monitoring, and support of airway, breathing, and circulation. Heat stroke generally requires neurologic symptoms to be diagnosed (collapse, in this case), whereas heat exhaustion presents similarly but with an intact neurologic examination.
incorrectExplanation: nd E.

questionStem: A 60-year-o ld woman is brought to the emergency depart ment because of a 12-hour history of moderate, diffuse abdominal pain and vomiting. Two weeks ago, she underwe nt a sigmoidectomy for perforated diverticulitis. Her postoperative course has been otherwise uncomplicated. She has not had fever, diarrhea, or pain with urination. Her last bowel movement yesterday was normal. She has not passed any flatus today. Her medications are ciprofloxacin, metronidazole, and oxycodone-acetaminophen. On arrival, the patient is in moderate distress. She is awake and alert. Her temperature is 37.9°C (100.2°F), pulse is 100/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 140/65 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 98%. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnorma lities. The abdomen is moderately distended and diffusely tender to palpation in all four quadrants. The surgical incision is clean, dry, and intact. Bowel sounds are decreased. An x-ray of the abdomen shows multiple loops of distended small bowel with air-fluid levels throughout; no air is noted in the rectum. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Bowel obstruction is the most likely diagnosis in a patient with previous abdominal surgery presenting with abdominal pain and obstipation. Obstruction of the bowel occurs from partial or complete blockage of the bowel lumen and typically presents with nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. Partial obstruction allows a degree of continued flatus with diminished stooling, and complete obstruction will result in obstipation (no passage of stool or flatus). Obstruction has many potential causes, although the most common are postsurgical peritoneal adhesions and hernias. On physical examination, patients typically present with abdominal tenderness, distention, tympany to percussion, and borborygmi (high-pitched, hyperactive bowel sounds). Potential complications include bowel rupture and necrosis, which can result in sudden-onset peritoneal signs such as rebound tenderness and guarding. X-ray of the abdomen typically discloses multiple air-fluid levels in the setting of dilated bowel loops. Management requires bowel rest, insertion of a nasogastric tube for decompression, and intravenous hydration followed by surgical intervention if the obstruction does not autoreduce. Partial obstruction may resolve with monitoring, supportive care, and bowel rest, whereas complete obstruction or any complicated partial obstruction generally requires management through exploratory laparotomy.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Complete blood count (Choice A) can be done as part of routine blood work prior to possible surgery or hospitalization, but it would not change or assist in the management.

questionStem: A 68-year-o ld man comes to the emergency department because of a 2-week history of abdom inal cramps after eating. He has also noticed a 2.3- kg (5-lb) weight loss during this time. He has had occasional loose stools but does not report any blood. He has hypertension and congestive heart failure. Medications are metopro lol, digoxin, and amlodipine. His medical records from 6 months ago show a left ventricu lar ejection fraction of 20%. He has no known drug allergies. On arrival, he appears thin and uncomfortable. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 96/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 138/72 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 97%. Cardiopu lmonary examination discloses an S3 and bilateral basilar crackles. The abdomen is soft with minimal genera lized tenderness to palpation. The remainder of the examination shows no abnorma lities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnos is?

choices.E: Upper gastrointest inal series with small bowel follow through

correctExplanation: CT angiography is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis. This patient with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), recent weight loss, and postprandial abdominal pain most likely has nonocclusive mesenteric ischemia. Mesenteric ischemia can occur secondary to thrombosis of the mesenteric artery or can result from low-flow cardiac states leading to intestinal hypoperfusion. The blood supply to the intestines is primarily derived from the superior mesenteric artery (SMA) and inferior mesenteric artery (IMA). Following a meal, the blood flow to the intestines increases to aid in the digestive process. In nonocclusive mesenteric ischemia, constriction of the mesenteric artery in combination with a decreased cardiac output leads to a supply-demand mismatch and subsequent intestina l ischemia. This is often experienced as postprandia l pain which may make some patients avoid eating altogether, thereby leading to weight loss. The diagnosis is made by CT angiography, which shows narrowing of the mesenteric vessels and their branches. When the condition is secondary to HFrEF, therapy is aimed at improving cardiac function.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Abdomina l ultrasonography (Choice A) can be used to evaluate the abdominal aorta and flow through its main branches, which include the SMA, IMA, and celiac trunk, but advanced cross-sectional imaging with CT angiography is more sensitive and specific for mesenteric ischemia. Barium enema (Choice B) is used infrequent ly in current clinical practice, but it can occasionally help to diagnose malrotation or volvulus. It is not helpful in the diagnosis of mesenteric ischemia. - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - .

questionStem: A previous ly healthy 32-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after the sudden onset of dizziness, numbness, and neck pain. She was participating in a vigorous aerobics class when she began to have sharp pain on the right side of her neck that spread to the back of her head, followed by a sensation of spinning and left-sided numbness. She is alert and oriented to person, place, and time. Her temperatu re is 37.6°C (99.7°F), pulse is 90/min and regular, and blood pressure is 130/80 mm Hg. Examination shows mild narrowing of the right palpebral fissure. The right pupil is 2 mm, and the left pupil is 4 mm; both pupils are reactive to light. Ocular movements are full. Funduscop ic examination shows no abnormalities. The palate does not elevate on the right, and the tongue protrudes in the midline. Muscle strength is full. Deep tendon reflexes are 2+ throughout. Babinski sign is absent. Sensation to pinprick is decreased over the entire left side of the body and right side of the face. Sensation to vibration and proprioception are intact. There is an intention tremor of the right upper extremity. Her gait is mildly ataxic. Her speech is mildly slurred. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Vertebral artery dissection is the most common cause of stroke in young, healthy patients and can be caused by spontaneous dissection or can be secondary to trauma. Even mild trauma such as quickly turning the neck, exercise, or chiropractic activities can be associated with vertebral artery dissection. Patients can present with symptoms such as neck pain, Horner syndrome, cranial neuropathies, dysarthria, and ataxia. Horner syndrome is characterized by the triad of ipsilateral miosis, ptosis (eg, narrowed palpebral fissure), and anhidrosis. Horner syndrome can arise from lesions along a sympathetic pathway. Vertebral artery dissection is associated with lateral medullary infarction or Wallenberg syndrome, characterized by ipsilateral ataxia of extremity movements and gait ataxia, and can be associated with nystagmus and dysarthria.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Carotid artery occlusion (Choice A) can cause decreased flow to the brain or embolic events resulting in cerebrovascular ischemia. Patients can have a carotid bruit on examination. Carotid plaques can embolize to cause ocular ischemia, contralateral hemiparesis, hemisensory loss, or homonymous hemianopsia. Cerebral vasculitis (Choice B) is rare and can present with neurologic deficits, headache, seizures, or coma. Symptoms of dizziness, neck pain, cranial nerve deficits, ataxia, and dysarthria are more consistent with vertebra l artery dissection.

questionStem: A 54-year-o ld man with type 2 diabetes mellitus is brought to the emergency department by paramedics 30 minutes after his wife found him lying unresponsive on the bed. His fingerstick blood glucose concentration was 20 mg/dl (1.11 mmol/L), so she called 911. His medicat ions are glimepiride and metformin. He has no known drug allergies. At the scene, paramedics could not obtain intravenous access and transported him to the hospita l. On arrival, the patient is diaphoretic and moaning softly. He does not cooperate w ith the examination. His temperature is 34.8°C (94.6°F), pulse is 90/min, respirations are 8/min, and blood pressure is 134/86 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 96%. Cardiopu lmonary examinat ion shows no abnorma lities. No skin rashes are noted. Now, fingerstick blood glucose concentration is 15 mg/dl (0.83 mmol/L). The nurses continue to have difficulty obtaining intravenous access. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management while awaiting intravenous access?
correctExplanation: Intramuscular administration of glucagon is the most appropriate step in management of this diabetic patient with severe hypoglycemia and no intravenous access. The treatment of severe hypoglycemia in a diabetic patient requires administration of either carbohydrates or glucagon. If intravenous access is available, carbohydrates can easily be given as 50% dextrose. However, in this case, intramuscular glucagon is a fast and safe way to reverse hypoglycemia in a patient with impaired consciousness and no intravenous access. After administration of glucagon, the patient must be closely monitored and intravenous access obtained because the effect of glucagon is transient. After intravenous access is available, a continuous infusion of glucose will likely be necessary. Any patient with hypoglycemia taking long-acting oral hypoglycemics ( sulfonylureas in this case) requires prolonged monitoring or admission because rebound hypoglycemia is common.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Application of a warming blanket (Choice A) should be included in the supportive care of this patient after his underlying problem has been addressed. Any delay of glucagon administration in this patient will increase his chances of death. While the patient's respiratory rate is low, bag-valve-mask ventilation (Choice B) is not necessary at this time given the adequate oxygen saturation of 96%. It is more important to address the underlying cause of this patient's symptoms, which is severe hypoglycemia. -- - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - .

questionStem: A 47-yea r-old man is brought to the emergency department by paramed ics 15 minutes after he was involved in a motor vehicle collision in which he was the restrained driver. The patient was traveling at about 5 miles per hour (8 km/hr) in a parking lot when his car struck a parked vehicle. Paramedics say that the damage to both vehicles was minimal. The, patient says he consumed two beers earlier in the evening. On arrival, he is awake, alert, and fully oriented. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 88/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 124/78 mm Hg. Examination shows tenderness and swelling of the right elbow but no other abnormal ities. The physician recomme nds that an x-ray of the elbow be performed. The patient says that he would prefer to leave; he is able to verba lize the risks of leaving using his own words. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in manageme nt?

choices.A: Allow the patient to leave against medica l advice
choices.C: Detain the patient until his blood alcohol concentratio n is measured
choices.D: Discharge the patient with a diagnosis of elbow contusion
choices.E: Obtain x-rays despite the patient's wishes

correctExplanation: Patient autonomy is one of four common medical ethical principles, along with beneficence, nonmaleficence, and justice. Autonomy posits that patients have the right to make their decisions provided that they have the capacity to do so and that they have been provided with appropriate information for use in making such a decision. A consenting adult with decision-making capacity has the right to refuse some or all aspects of medical care even if such a decision may result in short- or long-term morbidity or mortality. In this case, the patient is declining further work-up and treatment of a musculoskeleta l injury induced by a motor vehicle collision. Provided that this patient has capacity and that the caring physician has explained the benefits, risks, and alternatives of not performing the x-ray of the elbow, the patient may elect to refuse and then be allowed to leave against medical advice.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. It is not necessary to call the police (Choice B) in this case because the patient has demonstrated lawful behavior in the emergency department since arrival. It is not the physician's role to determine whether the police need to be involved in the motor vehicle collision, and disclosing such would be a breach of patient privacy. If the patient had assaulted providers who wished to pursue legal action, or if he had committed a reportable offense (eg, discharged a firearm), calling the police may be appropriate. Detaining the patient until his blood alcohol concentration is measured (Choice C) or obtaining x-rays despite the patient's wishes (Choice E) violates the ethical principle of patient autonomy. Because this patient demonstrates decision-making capacity by being able to verbalize the risks of leaving in his own words (and is not suspected to be impaired), there is no justification to detain the patient or perform tests against his will.

questionStem: A 72-year-o ld woman is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after losing consciousness while eating at home. During the past month, she has had intermittent 1-minute episodes of vertigo, nausea, double vision, and numbness of the left side of her face. She has a 20-year history of hypertension treated with enalapril. On arrival, she is intubated and mechanical ly ventilated because of poor respiratory effort. She is unrespons ive to commands. Her temperatu re is 37.1 °C (98.8°F), pulse is 72/min, and blood pressure is 160/94 mm Hg; she is overriding the ventilator with respirations of 14/min. The pupils are pinpoint. There are no horizontal eye moveme nts spontaneous ly or on doll's eye (oculocephal ic) maneuver. There are no spontaneous movements of the extremities except for occasiona l extensor posturing. Deep tendon reflexes are 2+ throughout. Babinski sign is present bilaterally. A complete blood count and serum electrolyte and glucose concentrations are within the reference ranges. A CT scan of the head within 2 hours of arrival shows no abnorma lities. Wh ich of the following is the most likely mechanism of these findings?
correctExplanation: This patient is showing signs of brainstem dysfunction including altered level of consciousness, poor respiratory effort, posturing, and negative oculocephalic maneuver on examination. Dysfunction of the brainstem can also present with cranial nerve dysfunction, dizziness, vertigo, and gait instability, symptoms that the patient had been experiencing prior to this acute episode. The Babinski sign, or extensor plantar response, is an upper motor neuron sign that indicates damage to the corticospinal tract, a descending motor tract located in the central nervous system. The Babinski sign is present when the lateral part of the plantar surface of the foot is firmly stroked and the hallux extends (moves rostrally) while the other toes abduct. The doll's eye (oculocephalic) maneuver refers to the brainstem reflex that occurs in normal adults in which the examiner moves the patient's head, and the eyes move in the opposite direction to hold the patient's gaze on an object. In a negative oculocephalic reflex, the patient's eyes remain midline, which indicates severe brainstem dysfunction. The cause of brainstem dysfunction in this patient is likely brainstem ischemia, which is often not disclosed on CT scan when acute. MRI is more sensitive for diagnosis. Patients with brainstem ischemia can have a stuttering course, which this patient experienced with mild intermittent symptoms prior to this presentation.

questionStem: A 37-year-o ld man is brought to the emergency department by paramedics 40 minutes after he sustained a stab wound to the chest during an altercation. He appears anxious and is in respiratory distress . His pulse is 130/min, respirations are 28/min, and blood pressure is 80/58 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 84%. He receives 100% oxygen by nonrebreather face mask. Examination shows jugular venous distention. There is a 2-cm wound over the left anterior chest wall but no active bleeding. correctExplanation: Tension pneumothorax can be a complication of a penetrating thoracic trauma and occurs when air is able to enter the pleural space but is prevented from exiting. Increasing amounts of trapped air in the pleural space compress the lung parenchyma, creating an inability for the lung to expand and causing it to collapse. As the pneumothorax progresses and continues to increase in size, it can result in tracheal and/or mediastina l deviation away from the affected hemithorax. It can result in decreased venous return to the heart, which manifests with hypotension and obstructive shock. Tension pneumothorax is characterized by absent breath sounds and hyperresonance to percussion caused by the increased air in the intrathoracic space displacing normal lung parenchyma. In cases of acute tension pneumothorax, evacuating the accumulated air via needle decompression and aspiration permits expansion of the lung and eliminates tension on the mediastinal structures, resolving obstructive shock. Immediate needle decompression is followed by tube thoracostomy, which promotes expansion of the lung, prevents reaccumu lation of air, and promotes healing of the pleural defect.

questionStem: A 26-yea r-old woman comes to the emergency department because of a 2-hour history of shortness of breath and moderate right-sided chest pain. She reports shortness of breath when walking up a flight of stairs this morning and when walking with friends at a shopping mall earlier. She also has a 2-day history of nonproduc tive cough. She has sickle cell disease. Her medications are hydroxyurea and acetami nophen with codeine as needed. The patient was hospitalized for treatme nt of a painful vase-occl usive crisis 1 year ago. On arrival , she is in mild respiratory distress. BMI is 21 kg/m2. Her temperatu re is 38.4 °C (101.1 °F), pulse is 104/min and regular, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 128/82 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 91 % that improves to 95% on 2 L/min of oxygen by nasal cannula. Fine crackles are heard at the right lung base. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglob in 8.9 g/dL (89 g/L) Hematocrit 25.2% Leukocyte count 12,600/mm 3 (12.6 x 109/L) Platelet count 457,000 /mm3 (457 x 109/L) A chest x-ray is shown. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's current condition?
correctExplanation: Infection is the most likely precipitant of this patient's acute chest syndrome (ACS). ACS occurs as a result of vaso-occlusion within the pulmonary microvasculature and is diagnosed in patients with sickle cell disease (SCD) who present with a new pulmonary infiltrate in the setting of fever or other new respiratory symptoms, including cough, shortness of breath, increased work of breathing, tachypnea, or hypoxemia. While ACS is a distinct clinical syndrome, it is common ly precipitated by another illness such as bacterial or viral pneumonia, asthma exacerbation with hypoventilation, or fat embo li, among others. It is both impractical and nearly impossible to distinguish ACS from pneumonia, so nearly all patients receive antibiotics to treat bacterial pneumonia. Additional ly, the use of either simple transfusion or exchange transfusion may be a component of therapy. Further treatment involves maintaining normoxia with supplemental oxygen or the use of noninvasive positive pressure ventilation, judicious use of fluids, and aggressive pulmonary hygiene measures, including the use of an incentive spirometer. Patients with a pulmonary embolism should be placed on full anticoagulation while all others should receive prophylaxis against venous thromboembolism. Pain should be managed aggressive ly.

Aplastic crisis (Choice A) presents with anemia and a low reticu locyte count indicating inadequate erythropoiesis, but does not present with fever, pulmonary symptoms, and a new infiltrate on chest x-ray. In patients with SCD, aplastic crisis can be precipitated by infection with parvovirus B19. Embolism (Choice B) should always be considered in patients with ACS, but thrombi found within the pulmonary vasculature are more likely to form in situ rather than represent emboli from the veins of the lower extremities. Fat emboli may also precipitate ACS, but these are not visualized on CT angiography and there is no treatment other than supportive care. Hypoventilation (Choice C) can precipitate ACS, but this patient 's prodrome with cough and shortness of breath is more suggestive of pneumonia than hypoventilation in isolation. Similarly, thrombosis (Choice E) can precipitate ACS, but this patient's symptoms prior to presentation suggest an alternative cause. Educational Objective: ACS is diagnosed in patients with SCD who present with a new pulmonary infiltrate and either fever or new respiratory symptoms. There are myriad precipitating causes, but infection is among the most common. In addition to treating any suspected underlying cause, further therapy should aim at maintaining normoxia, treating pain, and avoiding ongoing sickling with the use of simple or exchange transfusion.

If left untreated, PIO can become complicated by a tuba-ovarian abscess, as in this patient, presenting with focal tenderness and a possible fluctuant mass on physical examination. questionStem: A previously healthy 35-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of progressive redness and swelling of his right knee for the past 3 days. His temperat ure is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 84/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 134/7 4 mm Hg. Examination shows a 1.5 x 3-cm area of swelling and fluctuance over the anterior aspect of the right knee. A photograph is shown. Range of motion of the knee is full. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.B: Incision and drainage of the affected area

correctExplanation: Abscess formation occurs in the settin Score Report Lab Values Calculator Help Pause https://t.me/USMLENBME2CK Exam Section: Item 42 of 50 National Board of Medical Examiners ■ Mark Emergency Medicine Self-Assessment Correct Answer: B. Abscess formation occurs in the setting of an acute inflammatory response to an infectious organism, resulting in an organized collection of pus, necrotic cellular debris, and infectious organisms present on histology. A bacterial abscess presents with cutaneous erythema, warmth, fluctuance, and purulent drainage, often following inoculation from an injury such as a spider bite, puncture, or abrasion. Systemic symptoms including fever, tachycardia, and leukocytosis are often but not necessarily present. Most commonly, abscess formation is acute and results from a bacterial infection of the skin. The two most common pathogens to cause bacteria l infections of the skin are Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes (group A). S. aureus is most likely to cause a bacteria l abscess. It also causes impetigo, erysipe las, and folliculitis. Other less common organisms include C/ostridium perfringens, which infects an open wound and causes necrotizing fasciitis, Enterococcus faecalis, which causes nosocomial infections, and Pasteurel/a multocida, which causes infections secondary to cat and dog bites. Incision and drainage would be appropriate therapy for an abscess to release pus and debris to control the source of the infection. While the patient may also require oral antibiotics, without incision and drainage the oral antibiotics will not effectively penetrate the abscess wall; thus, it is the most important next step.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Biopsy of the affected area (Choice A) is not necessary in this case. Skin biopsy is performed when there is diagnostic uncertainty about the cause of a skin finding and can be used to obtain a sample for culture. It involves surgically removing a small core of skin and submitting it for pathology in formalin or for tissue culture in sterile saline. In this case, the diagnosis of bacterial abscess is clinical, and a biopsy is unnecessary. Oral antibiotic therapy (Choice C) is inadequate in this case without appropriate surgica l drainage of the bacterial abscess. While the patient may receive oral antibiotic therapy following incision and drainage, the bacterial source control provided by the surgical procedure is more critical than antibiotic therapy alone. Topical corticosteroid therapy (Choice D) is used to treat inf lammatory processes of the skin including dermatitis, psoriasis, and lichen planus. While the presence of erythema around the abscess clear ly indicates inflammation, treating this inflammation with topica l corticosteroids without treating the underlying cause, a bacterial abscess, will be ineffective. X-ray of the right knee (Choice E) is not necessary in this case because there is no suggestion of bony involvement of the infection. X­ ray of the right knee will not provide any information about the soft tissue surrounding the abscess. Imaging is unnecessary in this case, but if x-ray evaluation of the soft tissue was necessary, an MRI would be more appropriate. Educational Objective: A bacterial abscess presents with cutaneous erythema, warmth, fluctuance, and purulent drainage, often following inoculation from an injury. S. aureus is the most common ly identified organism. Incision and drainage is the first step in controlling the source of the infection and, without it, antibiotics alone will be inadequate.

questionStem: A previous ly healthy 37-year-old man comes to the emergency department because he has passed black, tarry stools during the past 4 hours. He had one episode of severe dizziness and palpitations when he arose from the toilet. He has not had abdominal pain or nausea. He has no history of ulcers. He does not smoke or drink alcohol. He appears pale. His pulse is 118/min, and blood pressure is 85/50 mm Hg while supine. Abdominal examination shows no tenderness. Test of the stool for occult blood is positive. His hematocrit is 37%. After intravenous administration of 2 L of 0.9% saline and transfusion of 3 units of packed red blood cells, his pulse is 100/min, and blood pressure is 100/70 mm Hg. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnos is?
correctExplanation: Upper endoscopy is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis in this patient with signs and symptoms of upper gastrointestina l bleeding (UGIB). Gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding is often separated into upper and lower GI bleeding. Patients with UGIB often present with dizziness or light-headedness, nausea, epigastric pain, and melena. Occasiona lly, as in the case of varicea l bleeding, hematemesis may accompany these symptoms. Laboratory findings may show an increased blood urea nitrogen concentration, but the decrease in hemoglobin concentration often lags behind clinical ly significant bleeding. Treatment should initially focus on resuscitation with crystalloids and erythrocyte transfusion as needed. All patients are started on an intravenous proton pump inhibitor, and patients with cirrhosis and suspected variceal bleeding should receive octreotide and antibiotics. Major causes of UGIB aside from esophageal varices include Mallory-Weiss tear, peptic ulcer disease, gastritis, esophagitis, and angiodysplasia. Rare causes include Dieulafoy lesion, gastric antra l vascular ectasia, and aortoenteric fistula. After patients have been stabilized, upper endoscopy should be performed both to determine the cause of bleeding and to intervene on any lesions that are amenable to treatment, such as bleeding ulcers or visibly bleeding blood vesse ls.

Resuscitation followed by endoscopy should general ly be performed first. If no cause of bleeding is identified, then CT angiography may be able to localize brisk bleeds that exist at locations distal to the duodenum. Colonoscopy (Choice B) is the intervention of choice when patients are suspected of having a source of lower GI bleeding such as diverticulosis or angiodysplasia, which often presents with hematochezia rather than melena.

correctExplanation: Exertional chest pain accompanied by shortness of breath that improves with rest is suggestive of stable angina pectoris, caused by cardiac ischemia from insufficient perfusion during exertion through narrowed atherosclerotic coronary arteries. This patient presents with symptoms consistent with unstable angina, defined by angina symptoms that are new, occur at rest, or are worsening in severity. Unstable angina is a type of acute coronary syndrome, which requires urgent diagnostic workup including serial ECGs, troponin testing, cardiology consultation, and myocardial perfusion testing, stress testing, or cardiac cathete rization. Nitroglycerin is a potent venodilator that decreases cardiac preload and myocardial oxygen demand, making it a first-line therapy in the treatment of angina pectoris along with aspirin, which inhibits platelet aggregation. Patients with unstable angina are stratified on the basis of the Thrombolysis in Myocardial Infarction (TIMI) score, which assists in identifying the need for therapeutic anticoagulation and coronary angiography. In this patient with improving chest pain, a normal ECG, and serial troponin concentrations within the reference range, the most appropriate next step in management is urgent myocardia l perfusion testing.

This patient is presenting with chest pain with similar episodes during exertion that is relieved with aspirin, nitroglycerin, and morphine, which is more consistent with anginal chest pain. Emergent cardiac catheterization (Choice B) would be appropriate in cases of acute myocardial infarction, which would present similarly with anginal chest pain but would have ECG changes showing ST-segment elevation and increased concentrations of serum troponin. This patient's diagnostic work-up shows no abnorma lities, making acute myocardial infarction unlikely. correctExplanation: Anaphylactic shock, a severe type I (immediate) hypersensitivity reaction, presents following exposure to an allergen. It is caused by widespread lgE-mediated mast cell degranu lation and is characterized by histaminergic responses within multiple organ systems leading to flushing, angioedema, bronchospasm, nausea, vomiting, abdominal discomfort, and vasodi lation, which can lead to airway obstruction and circulatory collapse. It is general ly acute in onset following a specific exposure and general ly does not self-resolve. If not managed promptly, death can occur from hypoxia and/or distributive shock. Anaphylaxis is a form of distributive shock, which is characterized by a primary reduction in systemic vascular resistance (SVR). This reduction in SVR is secondary to lgE-mediated histamine and cytokine release. Cardiac output increases to compensate for low SVR in the early stages of distributive shock. If the inciting state is not appropriate ly treated, further decompensation can occur, resulting in progressive hypotension and insufficient perfusion with associated end-organ damage. After the administration of epinephrine, fluid resuscitation should be initiated to increase intravascular volume to support adequate organ perfusion.
